stem: A 19-year-old man is reviewed in the Neurology Clinic following a seizure. Examination reveals eight café-au-lait spots and axillary and inguinal freckling. There are a number of fleshy nodules on his trunk and arms. Which of the following are you most likely to find on eye examination?
explanation: This man's presentation with epilepsy, café-au-lait spots(6), abnormal freckling and nodules consistent with neurofibromas is consistent with a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1.Lisch nodules are dome- shaped masses developing on the surface of the iris; they are gold-tan to brown in colour. Choroidal abnormalities and corkscrew retinal vessels may also be seen. Epilepsy is usually mild and seen in 6-7% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1. Q.

stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the Psychiatry Clinic for review. She was involved in a serious road traffic accident on the motorway one year earlier, in which a child was killed. On three or four nights every week, she suffers recurrent nightmares about the event and has flashbacks which have made her unable to drive her car, and she cannot travel in a vehicle with others on the motorway. She thinks about the event all the time and feels emotionally detached from her own children. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: This patient's clinical presentation is consistent with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD). Features which mark out PTSD include recurrent nightmares, flashbacks,avoidance of the event, rumination and emotional detachment. EMDR is an integrated psychotherapy approach which includes using eye movements to help the brain process traumatic events. Q.

stem: A 64-year-old man who has had type l diabetes for the past ten years comes to the Emergency Department. Over the past four hours, he has progressively lost vision in his right eye. He tells you this began on the lateral side of his right visual field and gradually spread like a dark curtain to involve all of the sight in his right eye. He had previous laser treatment to both eyes for diabetic retinopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The key features here include painless visual loss beginning peripherally and then progressing to involve the central region of vision over the course of a few hours. A possible trigger is proliferative diabetic retinopathy where neovascularisation is recognised to increase the risk for haemorrhage and subsequent retinal detachment. Retinal holes or tears can be treated with laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy. Q.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a rash affecting the flexural surfaces of her wrists and forearms. She complains that the rash is intensely itchy and, on healing, leaves small brown marks on her skin. Examination reveals small violet/red papules on the flexural surface of both wrists, with a white appearance over the top. There are some small white lesions visible on the inside of both cheeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her oral lesions?
explanation: The rash on this patient's wrists, coupled with the oral lesions, fit with a diagnosis of lichen planus. In the first instance, topical corticosteroids, either in the form of a mouthwash or a gel, are an appropriate intervention. Topical treatment using an ointment may also be applicable to the lesions on both wrists, although treatment is not always required for skin lesions, with spontaneous clearance a possibility. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has recurrent episodes of gout comes to the Emergency Department with pain in his great toe. His current medications are allopurinol 300 mg per day and benzbromarone (prescribed for him on a named-patient basis). Which of the following is the mode of action of benzbromarone?
explanation: Benzbromarone is a long-acting URAT-1 inhibitor which increases excretion of uric acid by blocking its reabsorption in the kidney. It can lead to a significant further reduction in uric acid on top of xanthine oxidase inhibition, thus reducing acute episodes of gout. It may be associated with a small increase in renal stone formation. Difficuty:Average.

stem: A35-year-old man attends the Cardiology Clinic for review. His brother died suddenly a few weeks earlier while playing squash. His brother complained of no symptoms before his death, apart from mild shortness of breath on exercise, and the patient himself has no significant medical illnesses. On examination, his blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg and his pulse is 88 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal, and his lungs are clear. Investigations: Electrocardiogram Sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy(LVH) by voltage criteria, two (ECG) ventricular ectopics noted on rhythm strip Echocardiogram Asymmetrical septal hypertrophy(18 mm across, left atrial dilatation and evidence of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy(HOCM), which is also the most likely underlying cause of death in his brother. The family history of sudden death suggests he may be at high risk of a fatal arrhythmia, although his age (30) and relatively mild septal hypertrophy imply a relatively lower-risk category. At this stage, therefore,an ambulatory ECG to look for short runs of asymptomatic ventricular tachycardia or atrial fibrillation may be useful in determining the need to progress to an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). The European Society of Cardiology(ESC) calculator for evaluating the risk of sudden cardiac death in HOCM patients may also be of value here. External Links NICE-Management of an arrhythmia bnf.nice.org.uk/treatment-summary/arrh... The European Society of Cardiology.⋯ ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28614597.

stem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of bilateral knee pain, worse on the right than on the left. She has a body mass index of 35kg/mand worked for many years as a cleaner.You suspect she may have osteoarthritis. What would you expect to find on knee X-ray?
options: Erosion affecting the lateral tibiofemoral compartment of the knee
Joint space narrowing affecting the medial tibiofemoral compartment of the knee
explanation: In osteoarthritis, the disease tends to involve the weight-bearing portions of the knee, the medial tibiofemoral compartment and/or the patellofemoral compartment. Joint space narrowing(3mm) is seen on weight-bearing, with subchondral sclerosis and marginal osteophyte formation. Subchondral cysts are also seen. Difficuty.

stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a severe sore throat, an erythematous rash and fevers which have increased over the last few days. He is concerned as he had unprotected sexual intercourse a few weeks earlier. Which of the following is the most important investigation in this situation?
options: Anti-human immunodeficiency virus(HIV) immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies
explanation: HIV RNA is the earliest detectable manifestation of acute HIV infection. Kits used to monitor HIV viral load in those with established infection can be used to detect infection. False negatives do occur, usually when the viral load is2000 copies, which necessitates retesting in conjunction with antigen testing. Difficulty.

stem: A 58-year-old man underwent a left temporal lobectomy as a teenager for resistant seizures.You review him in the Neurology Clinic. He is right-handed. Which of the following would you expect to find on neurological examination and psychological evaluation?
explanation: Features of injury to the dominant temporal lobe include receptive aphasia, dyslexia, impaired verbal memory and word agnosia or the inability to interpret words said to him. Complex hallucinations may be seen and contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia would be expected.This man is right-handed, meaning he is expected to be left lobe-dominant. Difficulty.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with recurrent bronchiectasis has been referred to the Immunology Clinic for evaluation and management of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). She has already begun scheduled appointments for immunoglobulin replacement. Which of the following infections occurs chronically with a much greater frequency in CVID than in patients without the condition?
explanation: Chronic giardiasis causing long-standing diarrhoea, malabsorption and weight loss has been reported in patients with CVID and is thought to occur much more commonly than in patients without the condition. Increased vulnerability to giardiasis is related to low levels of immunoglobulin A(IgA).Metronidazole or tinidazole are appropriate interventions for giardiasis. Difficulty.

stem: A 23-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. His 19-year-old brother was found dead in bed some four weeks earlier. The brother had no significant past medical history before his death, and the patient also has no significant medical illnesses, apart from one episode of syncope a year earlier. Cardiovascular examination in the clinic is normal. An electrocardiogram(ECG) reveals coved ST segment elevation of more than 2 mm in V1-V3, followed by a negative T wave. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged This patient's ECG findings are typical of those for Brugada syndrome type 1,which also fits with the sudden death of his brother. Cases of sudden death are seen more often at night or during periods of rest vs other causes of sudden death such as congenital long QT syndrome. It is thought to be due to a sodium channel mutation-over 60 mutations have been described-and it follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. External Links In some patients, there has been success in reducing ventricular tachycardia events by using electrophysiological mapping and ablation. The combination of epicardial and endocardial mapping and substrate ablation led to suppression of ventricular tachycardia in 98% of patients treated for recurrent events of ventricular tachycardia (VT) at four years. stem: You are examining the efficacy of a new L-type calcium channel blocker. In which phase of the cardiac action potential does the major amount of calcium enter the cell via L- channels?
explanation: During phase 2, delayed rectifier potassium channels allow potassium ions to leave the cell and L-type calcium channels allow the movement of calcium ions into the cell. These calcium ions bind to, and open, more calcium channels (called ryanodine receptors) located on the sarcoplasmic reticulum within the cell, allowing the flow of calcium ions out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

The Palliative Care team believes she only has a matter of a few weeks left. She is currently managed with 120 mg BD of morphine slow release(MST),40 mg of oral morphine PRN and regular paracetamol. She complains of worsening pain and yet is worried about the morphine making her drowsy and confused. stem: A 24-year-old type I diabetic woman comes to the clinic for review. She has recently decided to start a family with her partner. Her glucose is well controlled with an HbA1c of 47 mmol/mol. Medication includes ramipril 2.5 mg/day for microalbuminuria. Her current blood pressure is 105/72 mmHg. Her body mass index(BMI) is 22 kg/m You stop her ramipril. Which other intervention is most important to reduce the risk of congenital malformations in her pregnancy?
explanation: Women with type I diabetes are at increased risk of neural tube defects in the fetus, even when glucose and blood pressure are well controlled. For this reason, it is recommended to commence high-dose folic acid (5 mg) replacement at least three months before when a woman plans to try for a pregnancy. Q. stem: A 32-year-old nurse is reviewed in the Respiratory Clinic. She has been diagnosed with latent tuberculosis (TB) at a pre-employment medical. Which of the following is the correct intervention?
explanation: In patients aged 16-35 years who are human immunodeficiency virus(HIV)-negative,a3-month course of isoniazid and rifampicin is the appropriate intervention. Patients with HIV are thought to be at particular risk of peripheral neuropathy when exposed to isoniazid. However, co-administration of pyridoxine is thought to reduce the risk of this occurring.

stem: A 56-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He complains of shoulder pain and limitation of movement, having spent the weekend helping his daughter move into her new flat. Active abduction reveals pain between the 70-and 120-degree points of the arc of movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Rotator cuff injuries, including subacromial joint impingement, are seen after recurrent heavy lifting(eg after helping someone move to a new house). The painful arc,as seen here,is associated with subacromial impingement syndrome.

stem: A67-year-old woman, who has aortic valve disease and is under active follow-up of the cardiologists, is admitted with increasing shortness of breath and lethargy. A recent echocardiogram (ECHO) has revealed no significant change in her valve function nor in her ejection fraction. She is pale and looks tired in the clinic and has an ejection systolic murmur loudest in the aortic area. She has had both upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies which have proved normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 90 g/l 115-155 g/L Mean corpuscular 76 fl 76-98 fl volume (MCV) White cell count(WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Haptoglobin 0.6 g/l Normal Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
explanation: This patient has iron deficiency anaemia as a result of chronic GI blood loss. Angiodysplasia is recognised to occur in conjunction with aortic stenosis in the context of Heyde syndrome where coagulopathy is also seen. The coagulopathy which occurs in Heyde syndrome is thought to occur due to acquired von Willebrand's disease (type 2A). The underlying pathophysiology of the coagulation disorder is degradation of von Willebrand factor multimers because of shear stress across the valve. Angiodysplasia may occur because of alteration in the pulse waveform and hypoxia occurring as a result of aortic stenosis. The normal upper and lower Gl endoscopies point to the small bowel as the likely site of any disease, and a capsule endoscopy may be useful in confirming the diagnosis.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis and is commenced on pyridostigmine. Which of the following reflects the mode of action of pyridostigmine?
explanation: Symptoms of myasthenia gravis occur because of binding of autoantibodies to acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Pyridostigmine works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft, thus slowing down hydrolysis of acetylcholine. This makes more acetylcholine available at the neuromuscular junction,increasing muscle power. Cholinesterase therapy is usually combined with immune intervention.

stem: You are asked to take part in a trial of a new microribonucleic acid(microRNA)-based therapy for dyslipidaemia. Which of the following represents the primary function of microRNAs?
explanation: MicroRNAs target particular segments of mRNA to silence them, preventing ribosomal binding to mRNA and protein translation. They are becoming a therapeutic target to knock down production of proteins identified to be involved in the pathophysiology of disease.

stem: A72-year-old woman comes to the Palliative Care Clinic for review. She has carcinoma of the breast with bony metastases. Her General Practitioner has found it difficult to control her pain as when he increases her morphine slow-release(MST) above 10 mg BD she becomes excessively drowsy and nauseous. On examination, her blood pressure is 105/60 mmHg, her Glasgow Coma Scale(GCS) score is 15, although she intermittently appears to fall asleep during the consultation. Her body mass index(BMI) is 20 kg/m. explanation: Approximately 60% of the morphine dose is excreted in the urine after 24h and this patient has a significantly elevated creatinine(152μmol/L). Therefore, morphine and its active metabolite morphine-6- sulfate will accumulate.

stem: A 21-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with persistent haematuria. She has no significant medical illnesses and takes no regular medication. She tells you that her brother has blood in his urine and renal impairment, and also has hearing loss. Her blood pressure is 123/81mmHg, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Blood+, protein negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Alport syndrome is most commonly inherited in an X-linked fashion.This fits with the presentation of haematuria only in the 21-year-old woman, while her brother has hearing loss and renal impairment.X- linked Alport syndrome is caused by mutations in the COL4A5gene which encodes the collagen IV alpha-5 chain. Women with the mutation may only suffer haematuria and a slight deterioration in their renal function. Some subclinical high-tone deafness may also be detected. In men, progressive renal impairment and deafness are seen.

stem: A75-year-old man who is usually fit and well is admitted to the Emergency Department with drowsiness and shortness of breath which has steadily worsened over the past 2-3 days. He has been unwell over the past week with a diarrhoeal illness. According to his wife, he has found it increasingly difficult to walk and spent the previous evening sitting up in a chair. His blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg, and pulse 70 bpm and regular. He is drowsy and mildly confused. He has bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest. There is a 4/5 power weakness affecting both lower limbs, with diminished lower limb reflexes. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/L White cell count (WCC) 9.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 292×10/L 150-400×10/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 72 mg/L 0-10 mg/l Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO-) 22 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Pa(CO) 9kPa 4.6-6.0 kPa pH Forced vital capacity(FVC) 85% predicted Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation: GBS is suggested by the bilateral lower limb weakness with lower motor neurone signs and evidence of respiratory muscle weaknes. The recent lower gastrointestinal illness is consistent with GBS, as is the mild elevation in CRP level seen here. Lumbar puncture is likely to reveal an elevated cerebrospinal fluid(CSF) protein level, and electrocardiogram(ECG) abnormalities may be seen in some patients with second-or third-degree heart block. Intravenous immunoglobulin is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 42-year-old woman who has rheumatoid arthritis affecting her hands, feet and fingers comes to the clinic for review. She is complaining of pain affecting both knees which has worsened significantly over the past three months. You are concerned that she may be developing rheumatoid arthritis of the knees. Which of the following would you expect to find on knee X-ray?
options: Joint erosion involving the lateral portion of the joint
Joint space narrowing affecting the medial tibiofemoral compartment
explanation: Inflammatory arthritis of the knee typically involves the lateral or non-weight-bearing portion of the knee joint. This is in contrast to osteoarthritis where active disease predominantly involves the medial portion of the joint.

stem: A74-year-old man who has suffered multiple transient ischaemic attacks(TIAs) is prescribed dipyridamole modified-release(MR) because he is unable to take clopidogrel due to allergy. Which of the following represents the mode of action of dipyridamole?
explanation: Dipyridamole reduces uptake of adenosine into platelets, erythrocytes and endothelial cells by around 80%. There is then an increased concentration of adenosine locally which acts on the platelet A2 receptor, stimulating platelet adenylyl cyclase, thereby increasing platelet cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels. This is how platelet aggregation in response to various stimuli, such as platelet activating factor (PAF), collagen and adenosine diphosphate(ADP) is inhibited.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. He suffered an episode of viral myocarditis some 18 months earlier and has been left with an ejection fraction of 28%.Around two months ago, he began suffering from palpitations, and a 24-hour tape has revealed multiple episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT). Current medication includes bisoprolol and sacubitril/valsartan. His blood pressure is 118/82 mmHg,and pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest, and he has no significant ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 133 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.9×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Sinus rhythm, anterior Electrocardiogram(ECG) Q waves, QRS 132 ms Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has left ventricular failure with a low ejection fraction and episodes of recurrent VT. He is therefore at significant risk for cardiac arrest. Anti-arrhythmic agents may reduce the risk for episodes of VT occurring, but they will not abolish them completely. ICD is therefore the most appropriate intervention. When recurrent firing of the ICD occurs, anti-arrhythmic therapy can be added on top of the device. Evidence from intervention trials of ICD vs amiodarone have clearly shown that the ICD reduces mortality.

stem: A 28-year-old student is admitted to the High Dependency Unit for treatment of falciparum malaria. He is treated with intravenous (IV) quinine as initial therapy. Which of the following is the most important consequence of IV quinine therapy?
explanation: Malaria itself promotes hypoglycaemia, and quinine promotes insulin release. These two factors drive dangerously low blood sugar in patients prescribed quinine. Hypoglycaemia is therefore recognised as the main risk of IV quinine therapy and may require correction with either 20% or 50% glucose infusion. Seriously ill patients should always receive a concomitant glucose infusion with their quinine therapy.

stem: A72-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with severe confusion, drowsiness, nausea and vomiting. According to relatives, he has been steadily deteriorating over the past few weeks with a chronic cough and weight loss. He smokes 40 cigarettes per day. The paramedics have performed a 12-lead electrocardiogram(ECG) which has shown a short QT interval. Which of the following do you expect to be found on electrolyte testing?
explanation: The suspicion here is of an underlying bronchial carcinoma with progressive hypercalcaemia, nausea and vomiting. The short QT interval is very suspicious of hypercalcaemia. Other causes of a short QT interval include hyperkalaemia, hyperthermia and metabolic acidosis.

stem: A19-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has short stature, is obese and has learning difficulties. He has symptomatic hypocalcaemia, for which he takes calcium and vitamin D. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 122/82mmHg and a pulse of 70 bpm and regular. His body mass index(BMI) is 32 kg/m.You note that he has short fifth metatarsals and metacarpals. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 112 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Corrected Calcium (Ca+) 2.1 mmol/L 2.2-2.6 mmol/L Phosphate (PO-) 1.5 mmol/L 0.7-1.4 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The shortened fifth metatarsals and metacarpals, coupled with borderline low serum calcium levels and phosphate levels at the upper limit of the normal range, fit with a diagnosis of pseudohypoparathyroidism. The patient may also be poorly compliant with his calcium and vitamin D replacement. The syndrome is caused by a G protein-coupled receptor mutation which leads to parathyroid hormone resistance. Hypothyroidism may also be seen.

stem: A72-year-old man is prescribed omeprazole for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. He takes a number of medications, including ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide for ischaemic heart disease. Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is most likely to be seen in patients prescribed omeprazole?
explanation: Hypomagnesaemia has been seen in post-marketing surveillance, usually after at least three months of therapy. Medications which are associated with a reduction in serum magnesium level should be used with caution in patients prescribed omeprazole.

stem: A 21-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with lower back pain which has increased over the past four months and is particularly severe in the morning. The pain is improved by exercise and not improved by rest. He saw his General Practitioner in the last three months with shortness of breath which was thought to be due to asthma. Which of the following is the most likely finding on examination?
options: Limitation of forward and lateral flexion of the lumbar spine
Pain on palpation of the plantar surface of the foot
Sciatic nerve pain on straight leg raise
explanation: Limitation of movement of the lumbar spine is an early indication of ankylosing spondylitis, the most likely diagnosis here. Progression can be reduced by early instigation of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and physiotherapy to reduce fixed calcification of the spine.

stem: A74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with persistent diarrhoea and vomiting. He has chronic renal failure and takes digoxin, and you are concerned about digoxin toxicity in this situation. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most likely to exacerbate symptoms of digoxin toxicity?
explanation: Digoxin toxicity is worsened by hypokalaemia because digoxin normally binds to the ATPase pump on the same site as potassium.In hypokalaemia, there is more potential for digoxin to bind to the pump. Correction of hypokalaemia in digoxin toxicity significantly reduces the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with type l diabetes complains of severe tiredness, nausea, vomiting and weight loss over the past few weeks. She now feels too tired to attend her university course. Her diabetes is usually well controlled;however, over the past few months, she has had to reduce her insulin dose because of hypoglycaemia. Her blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg on lying down, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her body mass index(BMI) is 21 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 178×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 132 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 μmol/l 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 6.1 mmol 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 7.2 μU/L 0.17-3.2μU/L Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation: This patient's clinical picture with hypotension, tiredness, nausea, vomiting and weight loss, coupled with worsening hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, is consistent with a diagnosis of autoimmune adrenal insufficiency.The elevated TSH level also fits with the diagnosis. A cortisol level of420 nmol/l at 30 minutes post-ACTH test indicates an adequate adrenal response.

stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She has an intensely itchy rash affecting her elbows, knees, buttocks and posterior thighs. Apart from iron deficiency anaemia, diagnosed recently by her General Practitioner, she is well. Examination reveals a number of small vesicles, some of which have been deroofed to form small ulcers, particularly affecting her buttocks and the posterior thighs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Iron deficiency anaemia, even against an absence of gastrointestinal(GI) symptoms, raises the possibility of underlying coeliac disease.The pattern of the rash is consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis, which is also a feature of gluten enteropathy, although it is more rarely seen, compared with Gl symptoms. Strict avoidance of gluten is the intervention of choice. Dapsone may be of additional value in patients where symptoms are resistant to gluten avoidance.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is about to begin treatment for breast cancer with a trastuzumab-based regimen. She is concerned about potential side-effects. Which of the following is a major concern with trastuzumab therapy?
explanation: Cardiac failure is a common adverse reaction associated with trastuzumab therapy. The rate of grade II/IV heart failure is highest when trastuzumab is administered simultaneously with a taxane (around 2%).Across all trastuzumab trials, the rate of at least mild left ventricular(LV) dysfunction is around 4.6%,and in some trials in metastatic disease,the rates of cardiac failure were as high as 27% in patients taking trastuzumab in combination. It is thought to lead to cardiomyopathy because of targeting of DNA topoisomerase IIB. Regular echocardiographic screening is essential in patients receiving trastuzumab therapy, particularly in combination with a taxane.

stem: A50-year-old hypertensive man, who has a blood pressure(BP) measured at above 160/90 mmHg on three occasions over the past four months, comes to the clinic to commence therapy. He is Afro-Caribbean in origin and has a body mass index of 26 kg/m. He has no past medical illnesses of note. Routine bloods, including urea and electrolytes, are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy for him?
explanation: Hypertension in the Afro-Caribbean population is thought to be less responsive to intervention with angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors. For this reason, a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium antagonist, such as amlodipine, is the initial choice for controlling his BP. A dose of 5 mg should be used. There is little additive benefit in BP lowering by increasing the dose to 10 mg, and this is often at the expense of worsening of peripheral oedema. Calcium channel antagonists are also considered a first-line option for BP control in patients over 55 years of age.

stem: In cancer therapy, what is the rationale behind using combinations of chemotherapeutic agents rather than single agents?
options: Combination therapy can be given over a shorter period of time
Combination therapy decreases the chances of drug resistance developing
Combination therapy is less likely to result in long-term toxicity
Fewer side-effects occur in combination therapy
Metastases are less common in combination therapy
explanation: There are two main reasons for using combinations of different chemotherapy agents. Different drugs will exert their effects through different mechanisms, so combining them will increase the number of tumour cells killed in each cycle. It also reduces the chances therefore of drug resistance developing.

stem: A 45-year-old man who has alcoholism comes to the clinic for review. He has developed a blistering erythematous rash over sun-exposed skin, particularly over his face and upper arms. He tells you that when the areas of rash heal, they are often itchy and have increased pigmentation. He continues to drink up to 10 pints of beer per day. You confirm the presence of the erythematous rash with areas of hypertrichosis and hyperpigmentation. There are a number of spider naevi on examination of the chest and abdomen. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 155-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 105×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 89 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 123 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 235 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 18μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of his skin rash?
explanation: The big clues here as to the underlying diagnosis include chronic alcoholism,abnormal liver function tests and blistering rash on sun-exposed skin. It is caused by deficient action of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Avoidance of alcohol and use of sun barrier creams are important components of therapy.Venesection may also be required for treatment of iron overload, and chloroquine improves symptoms in some patients.

stem: A 25-year-old man comes to the clinic for review following planned splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. He has been taking penicillin prophylaxis since his surgery. For which of the following infections does the risk increase the most post-splenectomy?
explanation: The risk for infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae, N.meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae is particularly increased in patients post-splenectomy. The risk is increased up to 350-fold in patients post- splenectomy, although the risk for S. pneumoniae infection may be ameliorated with planned vaccination before splenectomy. To reduce risks for infection post-surgery, penicillin prophylaxis is advised.This increased risk for infection is thought to be due to deficient killing of opsonised polysaccharide-encapsulated bacteria. Risks for severe malaria infection are also increased post-splenectomy.

stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and type ll diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department with sweating, pre-syncopal feelings and dull retrosternal chest pain of 30 minutes'duration. He has suffered from increasing chest pain on exercise over the past three months but has not consulted the doctor about this. His blood pressure on arrival is 90/65 mmHg. His pulse is 84 bpm and regular. His jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated, and his chest is clear. Investigations: Standard electrocardiogram Horizontal ST depression in leads V1-V3, tall and broad R waves, with a (ECG) dominant R wave in V2 Posterior leads (V7-V9)-0.5 mm of ST elevation Where is the most likely site of arterial occlusion?
explanation: The posterior descending artery is supplied by the right coronary artery in around 90% of patients who have a right dominant coronary circulation. Occlusion of the artery leads to symptoms of posterior myocardial infarction and the ECG changes seen here. In the other 10% of patients, the artery is supplied by the left side of the coronary circulation.

stem: You are examining the site of action on the kidney of a range of diuretics and antihypertensives. Where is the site of action of spironolactone in patients already taking furosemide?
options: Descending limb of the loop of Henle
Ascending limb of the loop of Henle
explanation: Spironolactone antagonises the action of aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor, diminishing sodium reabsorption in the distal tubule by inhibiting the basolateral sodium(Na+)/potassium(K+) pump. Aldosterone action is responsible for reabsorption of around 2% of filtered sodium in the kidneys.

stem: A 62-year-old man is referred to the Oncology Clinic with a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), having presented to the general practitioner with tiredness and lethargy. He was found to have a white blood cell count of 39.2×10/L,which almost all comprised lymphocytes. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is associated with the worst prognosis in CLL?
explanation: The 17p deletion is associated with particularly poor outcomes in CLL. Both the 17p deletion and p53 mutation drive more aggressive intervention in CLL, although unfortunately only modest improvements in outcome have been made over the past few years. It is thought that patients with the 17p deletion may respond better to ibrutinib.

stem: A48-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic with thyrotoxicosis diagnosed by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level of0.05 μu and symptoms of tachycardia,tremor, sweating, weight loss and anxiety. Examination in the clinic reveals a blood pressure of 123/88 mmHg and a pulse of 89 bpm and regular. There is a fine tremor at rest. Palpation of the neck reveals a small right-sided thyroid nodule. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Thyroid stimulating hormone(TSH) 0.05μU/L 0.17-3.2μU/L Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
options: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck
explanation: Thyroid Cancer Media explanations This patient's symptoms and clinical findings are suggestive of a solitary ‘hot'nodule, a thyroid adenoma producing excess thyroid hormone. A thyroid isotope uptake scan will show uptake of the isotope concentrated in the nodule, with decreased uptake elsewhere in the gland. Diagnosis can pave the way for radioactive iodine as the intervention of choice.

stem: A76-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department with fever, shortness of breath and a cough productive of purulent sputum. Her temperature is 38.8℃, and blood pressure 122/82 mmHg. There are crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest, consistent with a right lower lobe pneumonia. Her respiratory rate is 25 breaths/minute. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 14.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 251×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 8.1 mmol/l 2.5-6.5 mmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 221 mg/L 0-10 mg/l Chest X-ray Right lower lobe pneumonia Apart from her age, which of the clinical features puts her at risk according to CURB-65 criteria?
explanation: The CURB-65 criteria are detailed below: · confusion of new onset(defined as an Abbreviated Mental Test Score(AMTS) of 8 or less) · blood urea nitrogen7mmol/L(19 mg/dl) · respiratory rate of 30 breaths/minute or greater · blood pressure90 mmHg systolic or 60 mmHg or less diastolic ·age 65 or older · risk of death for a CURB score of O is 0.6%; there is a progressive increase as points in the score are accumulated, rising to 2.7% for 1 point,6.8% for 2 points, 14.0% for 3 points and 27.8% for 4 or more points.

stem: A74-year-old man comes to the Haematology Clinic for review. He has suffered from headaches, weight loss and fevers over the past 4-6 months. He has developed a purpuric rash and is particularly concerned because over the past few weeks, he has developed intermittent blurred vision. He also suffered transient complete loss of vision affecting his right eye some three weeks ago. He reports that throughout the previous year, his health was good, and he still workks part-time in the family business.His blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg, and pulse 85 bpm and regular. He looks pale. Abdominal palpation reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 89 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 149×10/ 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 87 mm/hour 0-10 mm in the first hour Immunoglobulin M(IgM) paraprotein Positive Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This man's symptoms are consistent with Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia(WM). WM is associated with an IgM paraprotein and symptoms of hyperviscosity,including the transient ischaemic attack (TIA) reported here. The British Society of Haematology guidelines recommend a rituximab-containing regimen as initial treatment for patients who are able to tolerate it,and bendamustine plus rituximab is acceptable as initial combination therapy. Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody which targets B lymphocytes, and bendamustine is a nitrogen mustard which interferes with DNA synthesis.

stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department 48 hours after returning from a holiday to India. He is very concerned as he has gross haematuria when he passes urine. He began suffering from a sore throat and a fever some two days earlier. His vaccination schedule is up-to-date and he complied with all required vaccinations before going on holiday. His blood pressure is 115/80 mmHg, pulse 65 bpm and temperature 37.8°℃. His abdomen is soft and non- tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 10.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 311×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 95 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein ++, blood+++ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient's presentation with gross haematuria, only 48 hours after the onset of an upper respiratory tract infection, fits well with a diagnosis of lgA nephropathy. Patients may also present with chronic low-grade haematuria. It is thought that lgA nephropathy results from autoantibodies against lgA1 and that the condition is worsened by an upper respiratory tract infection. Hypertension in association with IgA nephropathy should be treated aggressively with angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors, and proteinuria should be managed initially with corticosteroids.

stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review.Her son passed away from a drug overdose one year earlier. She lost her job six months ago because of poor performance and has lost significant weight. According to her sister who attends with her, the house is dirty and unkempt and she is not looking after herself. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg;her pulse is 90 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 21 kg/m. Which of the following is most likely to be of benefit to this patient?
explanation: This patient has symptoms of depression which have gone beyond the usual six months after the death of a loved one, which would fit with the definition of a normal bereavement reaction. This fits with an adjustment disorder, and cognitive behavioural therapy to cope with the death of her son is the most appropriate next step.

stem: A32-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has suffered from progressive shortness of breath over the last two years. His General Practitioner has noted cyanosis and shortness of breath at rest, coupled with a systolic murmur. His blood pressure is 149/84 mmHg. His chest is clear, and there is bilateral pitting oedema of the ankles. Cardiac catheterisation reveals evidence of pulmonary hypertension with a pulmonary artery pressure of 45 mmHg. Oxygen saturation in the superior vena cava (SVC) is 75%,in the right atrium 75% and in the right ventricle 85%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Evidence of pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure and a step-up in oxygen saturation between the right atrium and the right ventricle is most consistent with a VSD. Ideally large VSDs(as here) should be closed early before the development of pulmonary hypertension. In patients with VSD who develop Eisenmenger syndrome as a result of chronically increased right-sided pressures, where reversal of the left- to-right shunt is seen, outlook is poor, with a significantly increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia and sudden death, with heart and lung transplantation as the intervention of choice.

stem: You are doing a research project on the response of individuals to chronic hypoxia at high altitude resulting in an increase in haemoglobin. Which organ drives most of the response to hypoxia?
explanation: The carotid body is found near the bifurcation of the carotid artery. It contains glomus cells, and type 1 glomus cells detect oxygen partial pressure. When the partial pressure of oxygen falls below 8kPa, output from glomus cells increases significantly via afferent fibres of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

stem: You are examining the performance of a new point-of-care test for detecting meningococcal infection. Which of the following is the performance criterion for correctly identifying meningococcal infection?
explanation: Sensitivity is the most important parameter when using a test for this life-threatening disease. It is important that no positive cases of meningococcus are missed. Yet some false positive cases may be acceptable, so the sensitivity should be set as high as possible in this situation.

stem: An 82-year-old man who is three days post-planned left total hip replacement is reviewed on the ward because of a cough productive of purulent and bloodstained sputum. He has right-sided pleuritic chest pain. His temperature is 38.8℃, and blood pressure 88/60 mmHg. There are crackles at the right base on auscultation of the chest, consistent with consolidation. Oxygen saturation is 91% on air. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 14.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/l 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 115μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Urea 18.2 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/l Chest×-ray Right lower lobe consolidation Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has hospital-acquired pneumonia, given his length of stay post-total hip replacement, with late- onset Pseudomonas pneumonia pushing to the top of potential differential diagnoses. Given the severe features, including low oxygen saturation and elevated urea levels, piperacillin-tazobactam is the obvious next step. In some areas, hospitals are moving away from the use of piperacillin-tazobactam, but the severe features may well drive an exception here. Where mandated by local policy,co-amoxiclav may be a reasonable alternative.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her sister. She is known to have a problem with alcohol and was found by her sister drunk in the pub, rather than attending her mother's funeral which had taken place that day. Her sister is very concerned because the patient claims that she is unable to see and is extremely distressed. Physical examination, including fundoscopy, in the Emergency Department is normal. The patient claims that she is unable to see even your fingers in front of her face, and is acutely distressed. Further review by the ophthalmoloist fails to reveal any physical abnormality. A CT scan and MRI of the head and neck show no abnormalites. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Conversion disorder is also known as functional neurologic symptom disorder. It is characterised by neurologic symptoms such as weakness, abnormal movements or non-epileptic seizures that are not consistent with a neurologic disease but cause significant distress and/or functional impairment. Symptoms are often triggered by an acutely stressful life event such as the one which occurred here.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Asthma Clinic. Her current management is 100 μg of inhaled beclomethasone twice daily.Yet she is still suffering from a cough, particularly at night, and is using her salbutamol inhaler too frequently. Her peak flow is 420 L/minute (550 predicted). Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing her asthma according to NICE guidelines?
explanation: Adding montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, is the next line therapy for patients who fail to gain asthma control on low-dose inhaled corticosteroids. Not all patients respond to such therapies so a review should occur 1 to 2 months later. Patients who fail this trial should be considered for the addition of a long acting beta agonist.

stem: A49-year-old woman is discharged from the Acute Psychiatric Ward a few days after commencing olanzapine for an acute episode of mania. She has mild asthma for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler but is otherwise well. Her blood pressure is 122/82mmHg, and pulse 78 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 25 kg/m.She is worried about side-effects of her medication. Which of the following is most likely to occur after a few months of treatment?
explanation: Olanzapine is well recognised to cause weight gain,insulin resistance and dysglycaemia over time. The summary of product characteristics lists weight gain as a very common adverse event associated with olanzapine therapy. Trials demonstrated that over 47 days of therapy,20% of patients treated gained 7% or more in weight and 4.2% of patients gained15% in weight. Aypertension Orthostatic hypotension is seen as a very common side-effect of olanzapine therapy. Hypertension may, of course, occur over time because of chronic weight gain, although not over only a few months of treatment.

stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the clinic, complaining of persistent breathlessness over the past year, worse on exercise, and a nagging dry cough. His General Practitioner has trialled a salbutamol inhaler for his cough, but this has had little effect. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medications. He smoked ten cigarettes per day for a period of five years between the ages of 16 and 21. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. There are bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. His body mass index is 23 kg/m. Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second(FEV) 80% of predicted Forced vital capacity (FVC) 80% of predicted Computed tomography (CT) thorax Reticular fibrosis with honeycombing Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: NICE CKS: IPF nice.org.ukguidancelcg163 This patient's symptoms, spirometry and CT appearance are consistent with IPF. Both pirfenidone and nintedanib have been shown to reduce progression of disease and are an option for treatment under the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines where lung function is between 50% and 80% of predicted.

stem: A57-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a darkened velvety rash affecting the back of his neck and armpits and with increased pigmentation inside his mouth. He has been losing weight over the past few months and has symptoms of indigestion. His body mass index is 27 kg/m, and he is mildly tender in the epigastrium on abdominal palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/L 135-175 g/l Mean corpuscular 74.2 fl 76-98 fl volume White cell count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Glucose 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of his skin changes?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Transitional cell carcinoma(TCC) of the bladder
explanation: This patient has indigestion, iron deficiency anaemia and a rash consistent with acanthosis nigricans. When there is underlying malignancy, acanthosis nigricans can involve the mucus membranes in 25-50% of patients. Gastric adenocarcinoma is recognised as the most common cause of acanthosis nigricans.

stem: A73-year-old man who has been prescribed aspirin for cardiovascular protection comes to the clinic for review. He used to work as a science teacher and is interested in the mode of action by which aspirin prevents platelet aggregation. How does aspirin prevent platelet aggregation?
explanation: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase 1 and 2, which leads to reduced production of prostaglandins and thromboxane A2. It is the reduced production of thromboxane A2 which then inhibits platelet aggregation that makes aspirin a useful prophylactic agent against ischaemic cardiovascular events.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who was previously fit and well is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedic ambulance, having suffered a tonic-clonic seizure. According to her husband, she has suffered progressive drowsiness and confusion over the past three days, suffering from a fever and symptoms of short-term memory loss. She is drowsy and confused, with a temperature of 38.4°℃,a blood pressure of 122/82 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. She is unable to comply with fundoscopy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 124 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 131 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein(CRP) 72 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Low-density areas within the anterior Computed tomography(CT) head temporal lobes, more marked on the left than the right Which of the following is the most important intervention?
explanation: This patient has symptoms of encephalitis, including a gradual decrease in consciousness, confusion and loss of short-term memory.The small rise in CRP level against a background of a normal wCC also fits with this.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic for her routine 16-week antenatal check-up. She has been feeling well and her pregnancy is progressing normally. She has no significant past medical illnesses. Her blood pressure is 118/83 mmHg,and pulse 65 bpm and regular. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. A urine specimen sent the previous day to the lab reveals bacteriuria. It is sensitive to nitrofurantoin and ciprofloxacin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines are clear that asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy, the diagnosis here, should be treated. First-choice options include nitrofurantoin (100 mg modified-release twice daily (bd) for seven days if glomerular filtration rate(GFR)45ml/min).

stem: A 25-year-old man is reviewed in the clinic with progressive muscular weakness, cardiac failure and arrhythmia. You suspect an ion channel defect within muscle cells. Which of the following drives initial generation of an action potential within muscle cells?
explanation: Post-synaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the neuromuscular junction are activated as the initial step in muscle cell depolarisation. This causes opening of the intrinsic sodium/potassium channel, with a rapid influx of sodium ions and a slow efflux of potassium ions.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward with a severe frontal headache, which came on gradually while at work. He tells you that he has had worsening headaches over the past three months particularly when he exercises or towards the end of the day. His blood pressure is 182/105 mmHg, and pulse 85 bpm and regular. He has no heart murmurs; his chest is clear, and his abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses. His body mass index(BMI) is 22 kg/m. Investigations: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for blood pressure control, given the likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 138 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 239×10/L 150-400×109/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.5 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 113 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Abdominal ultrasound scan Left adrenal mass
explanation: The suspicion here is of an underlying phaeochromocytoma leading to episodes of hypertension like the one which has driven this patient's presentation. Maximal alpha blockade is crucial in controlling blood pressure in this condition and must take place before proceeding to any surgical exploration of the lesion.

stem: An 84-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department, having been found on the floor by his home help and having been there all night. He has type ll diabetes, for which he takes metformin and gliclazide, and suffered a previous inferior myocardial infarction. On admission to the Emergency Department, his blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg and pulse 95 bpm and regular. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. He is drowsy, but responsive, and appears to be moving all four limbs. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Investigations Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/L 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.9×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 151μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L D-dimer 620 ng/ml 500 ng/ml Troponin T 320 ng/l 30 ng/l Chest X-ray Upper lobe diversion, patchy shadowing consistent with cardiac failure Electrocardiogram (ECG) Left bundle branch block
explanation: This patient's hypotension, with a significant rise in troponin T, left bundle branch block and evidence of left ventricular failure(LVF) on the chestX-ray, fits with a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. It is possible that he does not report or complain of chest pain because of his diabetes mellitus and consequent neuropathy.

stem: A 67-year-old man is reviewed by the General Practitioner (GP) one week after commencing ramipril 2.5mg for mild left ventricular failure after an anterior myocardial infarction. The GP is concerned because the patient's creatinine level has risen from 135μmol/L to 150 μmol/L. His blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg,and pulse is 79 bpm and regular. Which of the following is the most likely reason for the rise in his serum creatinine level?
explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors dilate the efferent renal arteriolar system, which can lead to a reduction in glomerular filtration rate(GFR) because of renal hypoperfusion. A rise of up to 30% in creatinine level or a fall of 20% in GFR is considered acceptable, as long as it stabilises on further monitoring. Greater rises in serum creatinine level should be discussed with a specialist and medication potentially discontinued.

stem: A 27-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a circular erythematous rash on his left thigh. He has just returned from a walking holiday in the forests of West Sweden. Over the past few days, he has begun to suffer increased lethargy and fevers. Examination confirms the large circular area of erythema and a necrotic central area to the rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This man almost certainly has Lyme disease, which is endemic among deer ticks in North and West Sweden and is sensitive to both doxycycline and amoxicillin. A ten-day course is usually advised for such acute infection. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines recommend when erythema chronicum migrans and a possible eschar are identified, as here, there is no value in waiting for serology before treating.

stem: A42-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with easy bruising affecting both upper and lower limbs and areas of petechial rash. Physical examination confirms the bruising. Abdominal examination is normal, with no evidence of hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 29×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 91μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: Given the absence of other abnormal findings, apart from the low platelet count, the most likely diagnosis is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). The disease is thought to be caused by both antibody-mediated platelet destruction and inhibition of platelet production. Prednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin are typical initial interventions. Secondary ITP is seen in association with other autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE), viral infections and infection with Helicobacter pylori.

stem: A32-year-old man who has immunoglobulin A(IgA) nephropathy is reviewed in the Renal Clinic. Over the last three months, despite ramipril 10 mg daily and prednisolone 40 mg daily, his creatinine level has deteriorated from 105μmol/lto 175μmol/L. Blood pressure is 122/82mmHg. He has persistent proteinuria, measured at 2.4 g/day. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 175μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine Protein ++,blood+ Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing his renal impairment?
explanation: This patient has progressive IgA nephropathy despite controlled blood pressure,full-dose angiotensin- converting enzyme(ACE) inhibition and a high dose of oral prednisolone. At this point,introduction of a steroid-sparing agents is appropriate, with cyclophosphamide and azathioprine the most studied. Trials have shown that combination therapy does improve proteinuria and hence is likely to slow worsening of renal function over time.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward. He complains of sudden-onset headache with vomiting. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15/15. Computed cerebral angiography free blood identified in both ventricles, with an 8mm cerebral artery aneurysm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation: The most appropriate management in this case is use of an endovascular coil. Coiling is typically preferred, having shown better outcomes in the long run. In some cases, however, patient anatomy (tortuous vessels or plaque in the carotid arteries) may preclude this procedure and the patient may need to be transferred to another centre.

stem: A 64-year-old man who has taken up golf in his retirement comes to the clinic complaining of pain over the medial side of his elbow.Pain is worsened by pronation and flexion of the wrist and forearm at the same time and is maximal over the medial epicondyle. He also has a tingling sensation in the fourth and fifth fingers. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected here?
explanation: Ulnar nerve entrapment is seen in patients with golfer's elbow, the diagnosis here. This leads to loss of sensation over the fourth and fifth fingers and weakness of grip strength due to loss of power affecting the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic some four weeks after prolonged bleeding following a dental extraction. She also reports that she has always suffered from heavy periods but thought this was just something with which she had to cope. She tells you that other members of the family, both men and women, have suffered from bleeding episodes. Physical examination in the clinic is entirely normal. Investigations: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count(WCC) 6.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 109μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Prothrombin time(PT) 12.1 s 10.6-14.9s Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 45.2 s 23.0-35.0s
explanation: The inheritance pattern for this patient’s bleeding fits with an autosomal dominant disorder. The most common form of vWD,type 1,which is responsible for 60-80% of cases, leads to a quantitative defect where 19-45% of the usual level of von Willebrand factor (WF) is present.vWF assistsin platelet plug formation by attracting circulating platelets to the site of damage and it binds to coagulation factor VIII, preventing its clearance from plasma. Desmopressin is the initial intervention of choice for minor surgical procedures in vWD because it increases the levels of stored factor VIIl and vWF.

stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is taking long-term low-dose corticosteroids and methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis and plans to travel with her husband for a 6-month stay in Asia. Which vaccination is not suitable for her at this time because of her immunosuppression?
explanation: Varicella vaccination is a live attenuated vaccination produced in human diploid cells. Its use is therefore not recommended in patients with a suppressed immune system, like this patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Where steroids can be discontinued, vaccination around one month after cessation of immunosuppression is recommended. Other live vaccinations not recommended include measles, mumps and rubella(MMR), Live influenza vaccination and yellow fever.

stem: A52-year-old man comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. He is increasingly tired and, despite working hard at the gym, feels that his muscle strength continues to diminish. He also complains that he is carrying more weight around his abdomen. His General Practitioner has checked a range of routine blood tests, including thyroid function tests, which are unremarkable. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 122/82 mmHg and a pulse of 64 bpm and regular.His body mass index(BMI) is 25 kg/m.There is minor proximal muscle weakness, and you confirm the presence of abdominal adiposity. He wonders about growth hormone deficiency. Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Arginine-growth hormone releasing hormone(GHRH) stimulation test
explanation: An IGF-1 level below the age-and sex-specific normal range is suggestive of a diagnosis of growth hormone deficiency. This test has the advantage that it can be done in the Outpatient Department, while a dynamic stimulation test is initiated. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, growth hormone replacement may improve muscle mass and proximal myopathy significantly.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Gastroenterology Clinic for review. She underwent a terminal ileal resection for Crohn's disease due to stricture formation some three months ago. She has recovered well but is still complaining of very liquid motion from her ileostomy. Her weight has increased, and she reports no significant abdominal pain. Her abdomen is soft and non- tender; her ileostomy contains liquid motion, and her surgical scar is healing well. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count(WCC) 5.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 287×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 88μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-reactive protein (CRP) 12 mg/L 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for her diarrhoea?
explanation: This patient is most likely to be suffering from bile acid diarrhoea as a result of the ileal resection. The lack of abdominal pain and the normal CRP level do not suggest there is active ongoing inflammation. Colestyramine is a resin which binds bile acids and is a useful intervention to reduce stool liquidity in bile acid diarrhoea.

stem: A72-year-old man with diabetes mellitus and a previous myocardial infarction comes to the Emergency Department, having suffered a collapse after lunch in a local restaurant. His blood pressure is 179/100 mmHg, and pulse 95 bpm and regular. Prominent neurological findings include tongue deviation towards the left when you ask him to stick it out, right-sided limb weakness and a loss of fine touch and proprioception on the right-hand side of the body. Facial sensation is normal. Which of the following is the most likely location of this patient’s arterial occlusion?
explanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with medial medullary syndrome, caused by an infarction which affects the paramedian branches of the vertebral artery. This leads to loss of function of the ipsilateral medullary pyramid, the medial lemniscus and the hypoglossal nerve. Facial sensation is preserved because the trigeminal nucleus is spared.

stem: A 49-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department following a mixed overdose of propranolol and benzodiazepines. Of most concern is his heart rate, for which he has been commenced on external pacing. His Glasgow Coma Scale(GCS) score is 10, blood pressure 95/70 mmHg and pulse 58 bpm and intermittently paced. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.5×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 105μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 2.8 mmol/l 3.5-5.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage this patient's hypoglycaemia?
explanation: Beta-Blocker Overdose Media explanations Glucagon is recognised to treat both bradycardia associated with beta blocker overdose and hypoglycaemia. However,repeated doses are often required, and side-effects of glucagon therapy include nausea and vomiting. In this case, it will improve glucose levels and may well reduce the requirement for firing of the external pacemaker.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He received eradication therapy some three years earlier for Helicobacter pylori after presenting with dyspepsia. Over recent months, he has suffered from increasing belching and intermittent indigestion. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. His body mass index(BMI) is 25 kg/m.Routine bloods are also normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient should be retested for the presence of H.pylori, and in the event the test is positive, he should be considered for a further course of eradication therapy. It is well documented that H.pylori infection is associated in some patients with excessive belching and bloating. Usual eradication therapy involves a 7-day course of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) plus amoxicillin 1 g and either clarithromycin 500 mg or metronidazole 400 mg-all three given twice a day.

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a sudden-onset headache and bitemporal hemianopia. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals pituitary haemorrhage. What hormone is the most important to replace initially?
explanation: This patient has pituitary apoplexy where adrenal insufficiency is seen in a minimum of 60% of patients who suffer pituitary haemorrhage. Initiating cortisol replacement is the most important first step, because beginning replacement for other deficiencies, eg with thyroxine, can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

stem: A56-year-old man who runs a bar in Spain comes to the clinic for review on a trip back to the United Kingdom. He complains of chronic epigastric pain which radiates to his back, coupled with diarrhoea. This has been continuing for at least the past six months. His General Practitioner in Spain has prescribed him tramadol to manage the pain, which he now takes every day. He has lost 7 kg in weight over the past year. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and admits to drinking alcohol every evening. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular.The abdomen is soft, with no masses, and his body mass index(BMI) is 20 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 102 g/l 135-175 g/L Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 104 fl 76-98 fl White cell count(WCC) 6.7×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 118×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 88μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 129 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Albumin 26 g/L 35-55 g/l Bilirubin 13 μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Glucose 7.1 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Which of the following is the most useful investigation?
explanation: Anti-TTG antibodies are used to confirm a diagnosis of gluten enteropathy. In this case, although malabsorption could point us towards this as an underlying diagnosis, the epigastric pain radiating to the back is much more consistent with a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis.
